extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and researchers interested in 4chan and Internet culture
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic description of 4chan's site mechanics, board-level rules, moderation practices, and content policies. Covers how anonymity, ephemeral posting, technical anti-spam measures, and community governance shape posting behaviour and content on different boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity / No registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration is not available, except for staff, and users typically post anonymously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In place of registration, 4chan provides tripcodes as an optional form of authenticating a poster's identity. Making a post without filling in the 'Name' field causes posts to be attributed to 'Anonymous', and general understanding on 4chan holds that Anonymous is a collective. Moderators generally post without a name; a 'capcode' may be used to attribute the post to 'Anonymous ## Mod', though moderators often post without the capcode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ephemeral posting / thread bumping and deletion
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting is ephemeral: threads receiving recent replies are 'bumped' to the top of their respective board and old threads are deleted as new ones are created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site's lack of persistent archives ('no memory') and threads' ephemeral nature shape community norms and contribution incentives. This ephemeral model is repeatedly cited as a driver of 4chan's meme production and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board-specific rules and topic dedication
rubrics_metrics.description: Most boards have their own set of rules and are dedicated to a specific topic (anime, video games, politics, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards are topic-focused and enforce board-level norms; examples include /mu/ for music, /mlp/ for My Little Pony fandom, /pol/ for political discussion. Board rules can differ substantially, producing varying cultures across the site.

rubrics_metrics.name: /b/ 'no rules' policy (except illegal content)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Random' board—/b/—has few rules and is described as having a 'no rules' policy, except for bans on certain illegal content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Site-wide prohibitions (e.g., child pornography, invasions, under-18 viewing) still apply to /b/. The 'no rules' policy also applies to actions of administrators and moderators, meaning users may be banned at any time, for any reason, including for no reason at all. The 'no invasions' rule was added after /b/ users conducted disruptive 'invasions' of other sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site-wide illegal-content bans
rubrics_metrics.description: Site-wide bans prohibit certain illegal content, explicitly including child pornography, invasions of other websites (posting floods of disruptive content), and under-18 viewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These site-wide rules are inherited by boards and are among the few consistently enforced prohibitions across 4chan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation structure: volunteers and janitors
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation is performed by volunteer moderators (roughly ~20) and a junior moderation team called 'janitors'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Janitors may delete posts or images and suggest bans but cannot post with a capcode. Revealing oneself as a janitor is grounds for immediate dismissal. Moderators often operate anonymously and may exercise bans at their discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripcodes and capcodes as identity/authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: Tripcodes are provided as an optional form of authenticating a poster's identity; capcodes can be used to attribute posts to moderators or staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tripcodes allow persistent identity signalling without full registration. Capcodes distinguish official moderator/poster actions but are sparingly used, with moderators often posting without them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-driven standards / decentralized governance
rubrics_metrics.description: The site's governance emphasizes community-decided standards: 'the power lies in the community to dictate its own standards' while site staff provide a framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle explains why moderation and enforcement vary by board and over time; community norms can supersede formal rules in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-spam and security measures (reCAPTCHA, Cloudflare, technical upgrades)
rubrics_metrics.description: 4chan has implemented technical measures such as reCAPTCHA to thwart spam and adopted Cloudflare following DDoS attacks; the imageboards were rewritten in HTML5/CSS3 to improve client-side performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures are presented as responses to spam, worms, and denial-of-service attacks and as attempts to improve site resilience and usability.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4chan Pass paid bypass
rubrics_metrics.description: The '4chan Pass' is a paid feature that allows users to bypass typing a reCAPTCHA verification when posting and reporting posts on the image boards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money raised from passes supports site operation. The pass effectively privileges convenience for paying users and was introduced to help fund the site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global Rule 15 (GR15) content gating
rubrics_metrics.description: Global Rule 15 (GR15) banned pony content outside of a few select boards, directing all such discussions to /mlp/.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GR15 was implemented to manage content flooding across boards; it demonstrates a site-level policy to confine certain popular topics to designated boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain split for work-safe vs NSFW content (2018) and reversions
rubrics_metrics.description: In November 2018 the site was split into two domains—4channel.org for work-safe boards and 4chan.org for NSFW boards—to placate advertising providers; all boards returned to 4chan.org in December 2023.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural change illustrates how business/monetization pressures (ad provider policies) can drive structural policy decisions about content segregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement focus: primarily clearly illegal content
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers and researchers have reported that enforcement on the platform appears to target clearly illegal content (e.g., child pornography), while much else remains untouched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A quoted associate professor: 'The only moderation on the platform appears to be for clearly illegal content… Everything else remains untouched.' This captures critiques that non-illegal but harmful content is often tolerated.
